milestones.title: the meter
milestones.task: Write call_cost, call_seconds, and the methods Meter.ask, Meter.fan_out, Meter.totals and Meter.by_step. ask(step, system, user, tier="small") sends one request with user as the only message and records a Call; fan_out(thunks) takes a list of zero-argument functions and returns their results in order.
milestones.checkpoint: python3 check.py shows this milestone as ✔. Hand values first: call_cost("small", 1000, 200) is 0.0005, a million tokens each way on the large tier is $18, call_seconds("large", 1000, 100) is 4.3. Then a scripted model: the recorded Call carries the step, the tier and exactly the usage the model reported, the request has the system prompt and one user message, sequential calls add up on the clock, and after a fan_out the clock stands at start plus the slowest branch (nested fan-outs too, and an empty one changes nothing). Then thirty seeded random call mixes: totals, cost and per-step rows must agree with the list of calls, and the clock must lie between the longest single call and the sum of all of them.
milestones.explain:
Before any pattern, a measuring instrument. Every model call has four numbers worth recording: tokens in (the system prompt plus everything sent), tokens out, the dollars they cost, and the seconds they take. The first two come from the response's usage. The other two are functions of the model tier, because providers sell a cheap fast model and an expensive slow one and workflows are largely the art of using each where it pays.

Cost is linear in tokens with different prices for input and output: call_cost = (tokens_in × input price + tokens_out × output price) / 1,000,000. With this lab's assumed small-tier prices ($0.25 and $1.25 per million tokens), a call with 1,000 tokens in and 200 out costs (1,000 × 0.25 + 200 × 1.25) / 1,000,000 = $0.0005. Latency is an overhead plus a term per token, larger for output (a model generates one token at a time) than for input.

The subtle method is fan_out. Work that runs in parallel does not add up on the clock; the wait is set by the slowest branch, the effect behind tail latency at scale. The simulation runs the branches one after another in Python, but it rewinds the clock to the same starting point for each, and afterwards leaves the clock at the latest finish. Two numbers fall out and you should keep both: seconds, the critical path (the longest chain of calls that depend on each other, which is what the user waits for), and work_seconds, the sum over all calls (what you would wait with no parallelism, and a proxy for the capacity you consume).
milestones.card:
Before comparing designs you need an instrument that records every model call: tokens in, tokens out, dollars and seconds. Dollars are linear in tokens, with one price for input and another for output, and seconds are a fixed overhead plus a term per token.

call_cost and call_seconds read the per-tier PRICES and LATENCY tables, already written. Meter.ask sends one request with the user text as the only message, records a Call from the response's usage and moves the clock on. The subtle method is fan_out: work in parallel does not add up on the clock, because the wait is set by the slowest branch. Here the thunks (zero-argument functions) run one after another, but each starts from the same clock reading, and the clock ends at the latest finish. totals reports both seconds, the clock, and work_seconds, the sum of every call. by_step groups the calls by step name.

call_cost("small", 1000, 200) = (1000 x 0.25 + 200 x 1.25) / 1e6 = $0.0005
calls of 1, 2, 3 s: in a row 6 s; inside fan_out the clock moves 3 s, work is 6 s

Read more: A4 chapter 13, parallelisation: sectioning and voting.

milestones.title: a chain with gates
milestones.task: Write chain(meter, ticket_text), returning an Outcome (status "ok", "gate1" or "gate2", the reply or None, and a reason), and chain_outcomes(p_step, n_steps, catch). The docstrings give the five steps, the step names ("extract", "draft"), the exact messages and the three reason strings.
milestones.checkpoint: python3 check.py shows this milestone as ✔. For ticket T01 the reply must be exactly the stand-in's text, made in two calls named extract and draft whose requests the checker inspects field by field (system prompt, user message, the FACTS: JSON) and whose input tokens it recomputes; for T04 (no order id) the chain must make one call and stop at gate 1; an id that looks right but is not in ORDERS also stops there; a reply that is not JSON, or has no order_id, is a gate 1 failure; drafts that omit the order or run to 41 words fail gate 2, and exactly 40 words passes. Over all 24 tickets 11 pass and 13 stop at gate 1. Then the formulas: the hand values above, no gates (all failures silent), perfect gates (none), and forty seeded parameter sets where the three outcomes must be probabilities summing to 1 and better gates must never raise the silent rate.
milestones.explain:
A chain splits a task into steps in a fixed order, each model call working on the previous one's output. A gate is a check in plain code between two steps that decides whether to continue; it is cheap, exact and testable, and it is where everything you can verify without a model belongs. The support chain has two model steps with a lookup between them:

  1. extract (model): read the order id and the issue from the free-text ticket, as JSON.
  2. Gate 1 (code): is the id a real order? If not, stop. No later model call is made.
  3. lookup (code): fetch the order. A database read is not a language task.
  4. draft (model): write a reply from the facts only.
  5. Gate 2 (code): does the reply name the order and stay under 41 words?

Token accounting is the point of the milestone, so the contract fixes exactly what each call sends: the extract call sends the ticket text unchanged; the draft call sends "FACTS:" followed by json.dumps(facts, sort_keys=True). That makes your token counts reproducible and lets the checker compute them independently. Here is a real run on two tickets, one that names an order and one that does not:

T01 ok     calls=2 in= 81 out= 38 $0.000068  ok
T04 gate1  calls=1 in= 41 out=  9 $0.000022  no valid order id

The second ticket costs about a third as much as the first (41 tokens in and 9 out, against 81 and 38), and it ends with a clean "no valid order id" instead of a draft about nothing. Without gate 1 the draft step would be asked to write a reply about None, and a model asked to be helpful about None will often invent an order. A gate turns a silent wrong answer into a loud, cheap, handled one.

The arithmetic of compounding errors

Suppose each of n independent steps is right with probability p. All of them are right with probability pn: 0.95 = 0.590, so a five-step chain of 90% steps is wrong 41% of the time. Gates do not change that 59%. What they change is how the other 41% looks. Let c be the fraction of wrong outputs a gate catches. At each step the output is right (p), wrong and caught ((1 − p)c, the chain stops, loudly) or wrong and missed ((1 − p)(1 − c), the chain carries on). The chain finishes without any gate firing with probability (p + (1 − p)(1 − c))n, so:

correct = pn    detected = 1 − (p + (1 − p)(1 − c))n    silent = (p + (1 − p)(1 − c))n − pn

Silent failures (the chain finished and the answer is wrong) are the expensive ones, because nobody retries them or routes them to a person. Here are the numbers for p = 0.9 and n = 5, from your chain_outcomes:

gate catches   0%: correct 0.590  detected 0.000  silent 0.410
gate catches  50%: correct 0.590  detected 0.226  silent 0.183
gate catches  80%: correct 0.590  detected 0.341  silent 0.069
gate catches 100%: correct 0.590  detected 0.410  silent 0.000

With no gates all 41% of failures are silent; with gates that catch 80% of bad outputs the silent share falls to 6.9% and 34.1% become detected failures you can retry or hand to a human. This is the quantitative case for the advice in chapter 13 to put a check wherever you can verify something without a model, and for the eval harnesses of course A6 that measure how many failures your checks catch.
milestones.card:
A chain does a task in fixed steps, each model call working on the previous output, with a gate between steps: a check in plain code that decides whether to continue. A gate cannot make a step more accurate, but it turns a silent wrong answer into a loud, cheap one.

chain runs the five steps in its docstring and sends exactly what they say, so token counts are reproducible. When gate 1 fails, no later model call is made. For chain_outcomes, treat each step as independent. It is right with probability p_step. Otherwise it is wrong and caught by the gate with probability catch, which stops the chain loudly, or wrong and missed, so the chain goes on. "Correct" means every step was right, "detected" means a gate stopped the chain, and "silent" means it finished with a wrong output inside. The three must sum to 1.

p 0.9, 5 steps, no gates:  correct 0.590, silent 0.410
same chain, a perfect gate: correct 0.590, detected 0.410, silent 0

milestones.title: a router and its threshold
milestones.task: Write classify(meter, text) (a (label, confidence) pair; a malformed reply is ("other", 0.0)), route(meter, text, threshold=0.7, tier_override=None) returning a Routed, evaluate_router(tickets, threshold, tier_override) returning a dictionary of counts and costs, and pick_threshold(rows, max_misroute_rate).
milestones.checkpoint: python3 check.py shows this milestone as ✔. Requests are inspected (system prompt SYSTEM_CLASSIFY, the ticket text as the one user message, step names classify and handle, tiers small and large); a known label below the threshold goes to a human after one call, and confidence exactly at the threshold passes; tier_override replaces the route's tier. At threshold 0.7: 17 of 24 tickets handled automatically, 2 misrouted (T23, T24), 41 calls. Along 0.5 to 0.9 the misroutes are 4, 3, 2, 2, 1, and a higher threshold must never raise coverage, errors or cost. Forcing the large tier costs more than 2.5 times as much for identical tokens. pick_threshold returns 0.7, 0.9 and 0.5 for caps of 10%, 5% and 20%, prefers the higher threshold on a tie, and raises ValueError when no threshold qualifies.
milestones.explain:
Routing classifies an input and sends it down a specialised path. It earns its extra call when categories need different handling or different cost tiers. Here a small classifier call returns label|confidence; refunds go to a careful handler on the large tier, account and tracking tickets to cheaper handlers on the small tier, and everything else to a human. Four details are the whole craft, and each is something the check can see:

  • A fallback exists. A label outside the table, or a confidence below the threshold (the minimum confidence at which the router acts without a human), goes to a person. "Your driver was lovely" is not a support request.
  • The threshold is a dial, set from an evaluation. Raise it and fewer tickets are handled automatically but fewer are misrouted; lower it and the reverse. evaluate_router measures that trade on the labelled tickets and pick_threshold picks the highest automatic share inside an error cap you choose.
  • Confidence is not correctness. T23 ("Refund please, and reset my password") gets 0.93 from the classifier and is half wrong. No threshold in the sweep removes it, because a threshold can only filter out the cases the classifier is unsure about. Multi-intent inputs need a different fix: split the input first, or have each handler say what it did not cover.
  • The router must be cheaper than what it saves. It is a model call on every ticket. A tiny classifier call on the small tier moves refund-only work to the large tier and the rest away from it.

The tier is where the money is. The same 24 tickets at threshold 0.7 cost $0.00327 when each route uses its own tier; forcing every handled ticket onto the large tier costs $0.00874, 2.7 times as much, for exactly the same calls and tokens. Prices, not token counts, moved the bill, which is the lesson the last milestone returns to. (Chapter 19 of the evals course, Cost, Latency & Quality Trade-offs, turns this into Pareto fronts.)
milestones.card:
Routing classifies an input and sends it down a specialised path, so refunds go to the careful, expensive handler and simple tickets to a cheap one. The classifier returns a label and a confidence, and the threshold, the minimum confidence at which the router acts without a person, is a dial you set from measurement.

classify parses the reply label|confidence, and a malformed reply becomes ("other", 0.0). route sends a label outside ROUTES, or a confidence below the threshold, to a human after one call; a confidence exactly at the threshold passes. evaluate_router routes labelled tickets through one meter and counts automatic and misrouted ones. pick_threshold takes the row with the highest automatic share among those within the error cap, ties going to the higher threshold, and raises ValueError if none qualifies. Confidence is not correctness: a ticket with two requests can score high and still be half wrong.

(threshold, auto, misrouted): (0.5, 90%, 20%) (0.7, 70%, 10%) (0.9, 40%, 5%)
cap 10% -> 0.7: 0.5 breaks the cap, 0.7 covers more than 0.9

Read more: A4 chapter 13, routing: choose the path, then follow it.

milestones.title: parallel fan-out, sectioning and voting
milestones.task: Write section(meter, text, parallel=True), majority(votes), vote(meter, text, n, tier="small"), majority_accuracy(p, n) and evaluate_voting(items, n).
milestones.checkpoint: python3 check.py shows this milestone as ✔. section returns {"pii": ..., "tone": ..., "policy": ...} in that order with steps named check-pii and so on; run in parallel the clock reads the slowest call and run sequentially the sum, with identical tokens and dollars. majority handles ties in favour of the vote seen first and rejects an empty list. vote calls judge k with judge_system(k) for k = 0 to n−1 inside one fan_out (so five judges wait as long as one) and returns the label and the votes. majority_accuracy matches 0.784, 0.83692, 0.901191 and the edge cases, and refuses even n; thirty seeded values of p must show accuracy rising with n. Then the experiment on the 200 items: one judge near 70%, nine judges better by at least three points, no panel above 80%, nine judges at least five points below the formula, tokens exactly n-fold, and the waiting time unchanged as n grows.
milestones.explain:
When work divides into pieces that do not depend on each other, run them at once and combine the results in code. Chapter 13 names two variants, and they answer different questions.

Sectioning
Different independent subtasks run in parallel: here a check for personal data, a check of tone and a check for policy matters on the same message. Each call is narrow, and the wait is that of the slowest. The tokens are the same as running them in a row.
Voting
The same question goes to several judges and the answers are combined, usually by majority. It trades tokens for confidence on a noisy decision.

Sectioning is a measurement you have already seen in the timeline of milestone 1: the same three calls, the same $0.000047, a clock reading of 1.072 s one at a time and 0.358 s together. Voting needs more thought, because its promise is a formula and the formula has a condition.

If one judge is right with probability p and judges err independently, a majority of n (odd) is right with probability

P(majority right) = ∑k > n/2 C(n, k) pk (1 − p)n−k

For p = 0.7 that is 0.784 for three judges, 0.837 for five and 0.901 for nine, which is why voting is tempting. The condition is independence. The 200 items in fixtures.py are built so that one judge is right 70% of the time, but a fifth of the items are "hard" in a way that fools every judge the same way (the same ambiguity, the same missing context), and on the rest each judge is right 87.5% of the time. A majority can never beat the 80% of items that are not hard, however many judges you pay for.

Go deeper optional: why the ceiling is exactly 0.80

Let h = 0.2 be the share of hard items. On a hard item every judge gives the same wrong answer, so the majority is wrong with probability 1. On the other 80%, each judge is right with q = 0.7 / 0.8 = 0.875, independently, so the majority is right with probability P(q, n) from the formula above. The panel's accuracy is therefore 0.8 × P(0.875, n): 0.7 for one judge, and 0.8 × 0.9981 = 0.7985 for nine. The extra judges only improve the part of the problem that was already easy.
milestones.card:
When work divides into independent pieces, run them at once and combine the results in code. Sectioning gives different checks to different calls, so the wait is the slowest one and the tokens are unchanged; voting asks several judges the same question and takes the majority, trading tokens for confidence.

section runs the three checks in CHECK_SYSTEMS in their order, inside meter.fan_out or one after another, and returns a dict of replies. majority returns the most common vote, the first seen on a tie, and raises ValueError for none. vote asks judges 0 to n-1 inside one fan_out using judge_system(k), and returns the winner and the votes in judge order. majority_accuracy(p, n) adds the probabilities of every way more than half of n independent judges, each right with probability p, can be right; n must be odd. Independence is the catch: errors that all judges share cap the gain.

p = 0.7, n = 3: right if 2 or 3 judges are right
3 x 0.7 x 0.7 x 0.3 + 0.7 x 0.7 x 0.7 = 0.441 + 0.343 = 0.784

milestones.title: orchestrator-workers inside a budget
milestones.task: Write BudgetedMeter.check_budget (its ask is given and calls it), plan(meter, request) and orchestrate(meter, request, max_subtasks=6), returning an Orchestration (answer, planned, ran, dropped). The docstring of orchestrate lists the five steps and the exact fallback strings.
milestones.checkpoint: python3 check.py shows this milestone as ✔. check_budget: a third call with max_calls=2 is refused with reason calls and is not recorded; token and dollar limits stop the next call once reached (having spent exactly the limit counts as reached); Budget() with no limits never stops anything; with several limits reached, calls is reported first. plan is one call named plan on the large tier and returns [] for a reply that is not a JSON list. orchestrate: two cities cost exactly four calls (plan, two workers, synth) on tiers large, small, small, large with the specified messages, and the clock reads plan + slowest worker + synth; five cities with max_subtasks=3 run three workers and name the other two in the answer; the default limit of 6 lets five run; an empty plan says so after one call; a call budget of 4 and of 1 give the two fallback answers above. Finally forty seeded combinations of cities, call budget and worker cap: never more calls than the budget, ran + dropped = planned, every dropped task named in the answer, and "Not covered" present exactly when something was dropped.
milestones.explain:
Parallelisation needs you to know the parts when you write the program. Often you do not: "compare the refund windows of the branches in this email" has two subtasks if the email names two branches and nine if it names nine. In orchestrator-workers a planning call reads the input and decides the subtasks, a worker call handles each, and a final call synthesises the results. The number of workers is now chosen by a model, so cost is partly under the model's control. Anthropic's write-up of its multi-agent research system reports that early versions spawned dozens of sub-agents for simple queries before the prompts taught the lead how much effort a query deserved (chapter 14). Prompts are advice; limits in code are law. This milestone builds two such limits, and a rule about honesty.

  1. A cap on workers (max_subtasks). The plan may be longer; only the first few run.
  2. A budget on calls, tokens and dollars. BudgetedMeter checks before every call: if a limit has already been reached it raises BudgetExceeded and makes no call. So a call can push the total past a token or dollar limit, by at most one call's worth, and the next call is refused; a call limit is exact. (A hard stop that must never overshoot needs an estimate of the next call's size; this lab does not guess.)
  3. The answer must say what it left out. Dropped subtasks are reported with a reason (limit or budget) and named in the answer. A summary that silently covers three of five branches reads like a summary of five.

Here is a real run of your orchestrate on a five-city request, three ways. Notice that the clock reads less than the work whenever the workers ran in parallel, and that the answer under the call budget degrades gracefully instead of failing:

no limits (max_subtasks 6)
  answer : Shortest window: Derby: 14 days. Longest: Bath: 60 days.
  planned 5, ran 5, dropped []
  calls 7, tokens 269, $0.00164, 4.74s on the clock (6.11s of work)
max_subtasks=3
  answer : Shortest window: Derby: 14 days. Longest: York: 45 days. Not covered: Find the refund window for Hull, Find the refund window for Bath.
  planned 5, ran 3, dropped [('Hull', 'limit'), ('Bath', 'limit')]
  calls 5, tokens 220, $0.00160, 4.74s on the clock (5.42s of work)
Budget(max_calls=4)
  answer : Budget reached before synthesis: Leeds: 30 days; Derby: 14 days; York: 45 days. Not covered: Find the refund window for Hull, Find the refund window for Bath.
  planned 5, ran 3, dropped [('Hull', 'budget'), ('Bath', 'budget')]
  calls 4, tokens 182, $0.00132, 3.50s on the clock (4.19s of work)

With max_calls=4 the budget covers the plan and three workers; the other two workers are refused (budget), the synthesiser is refused too, and the answer falls back to the raw worker results with a clear label. That ordering is a design choice worth noticing: the cheap workers ran before the synthesis, so the budget ran out where it hurts most. A real system would reserve budget for the final step, or plan in a way that tells you what you can afford before you start (the planning call is a good place to ask for a smaller plan when the budget is small).
milestones.card:
In orchestrator-workers a planning call decides the subtasks, a worker call handles each and a final call combines them. A model now chooses the number of workers, so cost is partly out of your hands, and limits in code, not advice in a prompt, keep it bounded.

check_budget runs before every call and raises BudgetExceeded with "calls", "tokens" or "usd", in that order, if the calls so far have already reached a limit that is set. So a token or dollar limit can be overshot by one call, but a call limit is exact. plan is one large-tier call whose reply must be a JSON list, else []. In orchestrate only the first max_subtasks subtasks run, and a worker the budget refuses is dropped while the others carry on. The answer must say what it left out: a summary that covers three of five branches reads like one of five.

5 cities, max_subtasks=3: 3 workers run, the answer ends
"Not covered:" and names the other two (reason "limit")

Read more: A4 chapter 13, orchestrator-workers.

milestones.title: the whole desk
milestones.task: Write process_ticket(ticket, model, threshold=0.7, budget=None) returning a TicketResult (id, status answered or human, reason, calls, tokens, dollars, seconds), percentile(values, q) and run_desk(tickets, threshold=0.7, budget=None) returning the results and a summary.
milestones.checkpoint: python3 check.py shows this milestone as ✔. Percentile hand values (including unsorted input, a single value, q = 100) and its three ValueError cases. One ticket at a time: T01 is answered in 3 calls whose tokens and dollars match an independent recomputation; T04 stops at gate 1 after 2 calls with reason gate: no valid order id; T06 and T20 go to a human from the router after 1 call; T09 and T15 are answered in 2; T23 is (wrongly but confidently) answered as a refund; the threshold parameter reaches the router. Budgets: max_calls=2 turns the 3-call T01 into a human ticket with reason budget: calls after exactly 2 calls, max_usd of a billionth of a dollar stops after the first. The desk: 16 answered and 8 to humans (7 by the router, 1 by gate 1), p50 and p95 at ranks 12 and 23 of 24, and per-ticket call counts that match the path; a max_calls=2 desk escalates exactly the seven three-call tickets, caps every ticket and lowers the bill; a budget nobody reaches changes nothing; a lower threshold answers more and spends more. Twenty seeded random subsets, thresholds and budgets check the invariants.
milestones.explain:
Patterns compose, and the composition is where budgets earn their keep. The desk handles a ticket like this: classify (one small call); if the router is unsure or the ticket is not a support request, hand it to a human; if it is a tracking question, run the chain (extract, gate, draft, gate) instead of a free-text handler, because the answer must be built from real order data; otherwise call the specialist for that label on its tier. Each ticket gets its own BudgetedMeter, and a ticket that hits its budget does not fail: it goes to a human with the reason budget: calls (or tokens or usd), exactly like a failed gate or a low-confidence route.

Two reports then matter more than the total. The first is where the tokens and dollars go. Here is the ledger for the 24 tickets at threshold 0.7 (aggregated over every call from the per-ticket meters, with your Meter.by_step):

step       calls  tokens in tokens out  share       cost  share
classify      24        777         82    39%   $0.00030     9%
extract        8        316         79    18%   $0.00018     5%
draft          7        290        196    22%   $0.00032     9%
handle         9        233        240    21%   $0.00263    77%
total         48      1,616        597          $0.00342

The second is the distribution of per-ticket cost, not its mean: a budget is a promise about the worst case. percentile uses the nearest-rank definition (sort the values, take the one at rank ⌈q/100 × n⌉), which is exact, needs no interpolation and is easy to check by hand: the median of ten values 1 to 10 is 5, the 95th percentile is 10. The p95 token count per ticket (159 here) is the number to compare with a per-ticket token budget; a budget well under it will escalate real tickets, and one far above it protects you only from runaway loops.
milestones.card:
Patterns compose, and budgets keep the composition honest. The desk classifies each ticket, sends tracking questions through the gated chain and the rest to a specialist, gives every ticket its own budget, and hands to a human anything that fails a router check, a gate or its budget.

process_ticket follows the order in its docstring and records calls, tokens, dollars and seconds from the ticket's own meter. Any BudgetExceeded ends in a human ticket with the reason budget: calls (or tokens, usd), like any other escalation. percentile uses the nearest-rank rule: sort, then take the value at 1-based rank ceil(q / 100 * n). It raises ValueError for an empty list or a q outside 0 to 100. run_desk shares one model, makes a fresh budget per ticket and summarises. Look at the spread, not only the mean: a budget is a promise about the worst case.

percentile of 1..10:  q = 50 -> rank 5 -> 5
                      q = 95 -> rank ceil(9.5) = 10 -> 10

Read more: A4 chapter 13, choosing, combining and costing.
